title: Jeremiah 4:5–18
context: A new section sounds the alarm. In 4:5–6 the LORD commands that the trumpet be blown in Judah and Jerusalem and the people flee to the fortified cities, “for I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction,” where “evil” means calamity. The foe from the north (compare 1:13–15; 6:1, 22) is not named in this chapter. Many readers connect it with Babylon, which later chapters name (for example 20:4; 25:9, where “the families of the north” stand with Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon); an older proposal linked these oracles with Scythian raiders, but that link is uncertain and debated. In 4:7 the invader is a lion and a destroyer of nations, and in 4:8 the people are told to lament because the LORD’s anger has not turned back. The LORD announces in 4:9 that king, princes, priests, and prophets will be dismayed. In 4:10 Jeremiah protests, “Ah, Lord GOD! Surely you have greatly deceived this people,” since they had been told “You will have peace” (compare the false prophets’ message in 6:14; 14:13). A hot wind comes, not to winnow or cleanse (4:11–12); the enemy advances like clouds and whirlwind (4:13), and the people cry “Woe to us!” The LORD pleads, “Jerusalem, wash your heart from wickedness, that you may be saved” (4:14). Messengers announce the advance from Dan in the far north and the hills of Ephraim (4:15–17), and the LORD concludes that Judah’s own ways have brought this (4:18). Both traditions hold that God rules over the nations he uses in judgment and that Judah is responsible; the site’s existing discussions at Judges 9:23 and Joshua 11:20 cover the wider question of God’s use of hostile agents and are not repeated here.

verses.text: Declare in Judah, and publish in Jerusalem; and say, ‘Blow the trumpet in the land!’ Cry aloud and say, ‘Assemble yourselves! Let’s go into the fortified cities!’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands that the trumpet be blown and that Judah gather into fortified cities. Arminian readers note that the warning itself is merciful: the alarm comes before the destruction, giving people time to respond, and the prophet’s message assumes that hearing and heeding are real possibilities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as sovereign over the coming invasion, announcing it in advance so that his people know it is no accident of history but his judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the alarm as urgent and real, and both note that fortified cities will prove no final refuge apart from returning to the LORD.

verses.text: Set up a standard toward Zion. Flee for safety! Don’t wait; for I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction,” where evil means calamity, not moral wrong. Arminian readers see God bringing judgment in response to persistent covenant breaking, using a foe many link with Babylon (compare 25:9), with the timing still allowing repentance, as 4:14 shows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD directing the nations as instruments of his just purposes while the invaders remain responsible for their own violence. Shared ground: both traditions read “evil” here as disaster, both hold that God rules over the nations, and both treat the foe’s identity as Babylon in many readings, with older Scythian proposals uncertain.

verses.text: A lion has gone up from his thicket, and a destroyer of nations. He is on his way. He has gone out from his place, to make your land desolate, that your cities be laid waste, without inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes: A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations, to make the land desolate. Arminian readers see the image of a predator as a vivid warning of the real consequences of rejecting God, consequences that follow from a long history of refusal rather than arbitrary decree.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the destroyer as moving under God’s governance, even though he acts from his own ambition, so that Judah’s calamity is neither chance nor outside the LORD’s rule. Shared ground: both traditions read the lion as the invading power, commonly linked with Babylon, and both see the desolation of cities as covenant curse.

verses.text: For this, clothe yourself with sackcloth, lament and wail; for the fierce anger of the LORD hasn’t turned back from us.
verses.arminianNotes: The people are told to put on sackcloth, lament, and wail, “for the fierce anger of the LORD hasn’t turned back from us.” Arminian readers see lament as the fitting response of a people who recognize the seriousness of their sin, and they note that sorrow can open the way to the repentance God desires.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s anger as his settled, just opposition to sin, not a fit of temper, and they note that lament alone does not turn it back without true repentance. Shared ground: both traditions hold that divine anger is holy and just, and both see sackcloth as the right posture before it.

verses.text: “It will happen at that day,” says the LORD, “that the heart of the king will perish, along with the heart of the princes. The priests will be astonished, and the prophets will wonder.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that on that day the heart of the king and princes will perish, priests will be astonished, and prophets will wonder. Arminian readers see leaders who misled the people now confronted with the failure of their assurances, a reminder that leaders bear special responsibility for the paths they encourage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the collapse of every human support, royal, priestly, and prophetic, exposing the vanity of trust in anything but the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as judgment on leaders who failed their office (compare 2:8), and both see their dismay as the end of false confidence.

verses.text: Then I said, “Ah, Lord GOD! Surely you have greatly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, ‘You will have peace;’ whereas the sword reaches to the heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah protests, “Ah, Lord GOD! Surely you have greatly deceived this people,” since they had been promised peace. Arminian readers often take the words as Jeremiah’s anguished complaint about false prophets speaking peace (compare 6:14; 14:13), which God permitted but did not author, a cry of grief rather than a doctrinal statement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often read the same complaint as Jeremiah wrestling honestly with God’s governance, sometimes compared with 1 Kings 22:19–23, where God permits a lying spirit as judgment; they do not make God the author of sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as prophetic lament, and both affirm God’s truthfulness while taking Jeremiah’s anguish seriously.

verses.text: At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, “A hot wind blows from the bare heights in the wilderness toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow, nor to cleanse.
verses.arminianNotes: A hot wind blows from the bare heights “not to winnow, nor to cleanse.” Arminian readers note the shift from discipline to judgment: earlier chastening was meant to purify, but persistent refusal leads to a wind that destroys rather than refines, showing the real stakes of resisting grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as God’s judgment that no longer separates chaff from grain but sweeps all away, a solemn warning that time for repentance is not unlimited. Shared ground: both traditions read the hot wind as the invading army, and both note the tenderness of “the daughter of my people” even in judgment.

verses.text: A full wind from these will come for me. Now I will also utter judgments against them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says a full wind will come for him, and now he will utter judgments against them. Arminian readers see judgment pronounced after long patience, a just verdict on a people who rejected repeated calls, and they note that pronounced judgment does not cancel the urgent appeal of 4:14.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the judge who speaks the verdict and directs the instrument, so that the invasion executes his decree of justice. Shared ground: both traditions read the full wind as coming at the LORD’s word, and both hold that God’s judgments are righteous and deserved.

verses.text: Behold, he will come up as clouds, and his chariots will be as the whirlwind. His horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us! For we are ruined.
verses.arminianNotes: The enemy comes like clouds, chariots like a whirlwind, horses swifter than eagles, and the people cry, “Woe to us! For we are ruined.” Arminian readers see the people’s cry as a recognition of guilt that comes too late to avert disaster, a warning to respond before judgment arrives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the overwhelming speed of the enemy as a picture of how suddenly divine judgment can fall, and they note the people’s cry as an honest admission of ruin. Shared ground: both traditions read the imagery as the invader’s power, and both hear in “Woe to us!” the voice of the people, not the prophet alone.

verses.text: Jerusalem, wash your heart from wickedness, that you may be saved. How long will your evil thoughts lodge within you?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD pleads, “Jerusalem, wash your heart from wickedness, that you may be saved.” Arminian readers see a sincere offer even as judgment approaches: salvation is still possible if Jerusalem responds by grace, and the plea would be empty if the city could not answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a real command that shows the city’s duty, while noting that Scripture also speaks of God washing and renewing the heart (compare Psalm 51:10; Ezekiel 36:25–26). Shared ground: both traditions hold that the command is real, that deliverance is possible through repentance, and that evil thoughts lodging within are the root problem.

verses.text: For a voice declares from Dan, and publishes evil from the hills of Ephraim:
verses.arminianNotes: A voice declares from Dan and publishes evil from the hills of Ephraim, places in the north through which an invader would approach. Arminian readers see news of calamity spreading southward as a final warning, the danger drawing nearer while there is still a moment to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the advance as orderly under God’s providence, each report confirming the word the LORD had spoken. Shared ground: both traditions read Dan and the hills of Ephraim as geographical markers of approach from the north, and both see the announcement as fulfilling the alarm of 4:5–6.

verses.text: “Tell the nations, behold, publish against Jerusalem, ‘Watchers come from a far country, and raise their voice against the cities of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Watchers come from a far country and raise their voice against Judah’s cities. Arminian readers note that the nations are told of Jerusalem’s judgment, making the covenant people’s fall a public lesson, and that the LORD’s warnings are given openly so that all may learn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD summoning distant peoples for his purposes, just as he governs Judah’s affairs. They note that the besiegers act at his direction without being excused for their violence. Shared ground: both traditions read the watchers as besiegers, and both see their coming as the consequence of Judah’s rebellion.

verses.text: As keepers of a field, they are against her all around, because she has been rebellious against me,’ ” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The besiegers surround Jerusalem like keepers of a field, “because she has been rebellious against me,” says the LORD. Arminian readers stress that the cause is Judah’s own rebellion: judgment is not arbitrary but corresponds to sustained, chosen rejection of the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the stated cause and see God’s justice in the correspondence between sin and penalty. They note the sobering image of watchmen guarding a field, now set against the city. Shared ground: both traditions read the LORD as the speaker and rebellion as the reason for the siege.

verses.text: “Your way and your doings have brought these things to you. This is your wickedness, for it is bitter, for it reaches to your heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Your way and your doings have brought these things to you,” wickedness bitter and reaching to the heart. Arminian readers see judgment as the natural and just consequence of chosen paths, God confirming the direction people have taken rather than imposing an alien fate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same moral logic and stress that the heart is the source of sin, so that only a changed heart can bring a different path (compare 17:9). Shared ground: both traditions hold that Judah is responsible for her calamity and that the bitterness of sin reaches the innermost person.
